endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Prior to the general deployment of an AI system, careful review and consideration must be made by the health system to decide whether or not to deploy an AI model into production.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Identify and document the tools, resources, and infrastructure available and needed to carry out validation testing and monitoring for relevant AI models, including responsible AI baseline tests.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Internal experts who did not serve as front-line developers for the system and/or independent assessors are involved in regular assessments and updates.

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: Also includes guides for determining if AI products should be clinically integrated or abandoned.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: Finally, all the findings should be reviewed to determine if the AI model is worthy of clinical deployment.

endorsements.title: A practical framework for appropriate implementation and review of artificial intelligence (FAIR-AI) in healthcare
endorsements.quote: For our health system, all AI solutions designated as high risk are escalated to the AI Governance committee where they undergo a multidisciplinary discussion.

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: Decisions link directly to the chosen disposition and to a postdeployment monitoring plan with predefined indicators (eg, misinformation incidents, user-reported confusion, complaint rates, follow-up burden, and equity gaps) and time-bound rereview triggers.

endorsements.title: Foundation for Artificial Intelligence-Driven Democratization of Healthcare Access
endorsements.quote: Chief among these implementation requirements is the development and operationalization of structured governance mechanisms designed to ensure that artificial intelligence systems undergo appropriate technical validation procedures, comprehensive clinical evaluation methodologies, and rigorous ethical assessment protocols before deployment in clinical settings where algorithmic recommendations or automated processes may substantively influence patient care.

endorsements.title: Enhancing Physician Resilience to Generative AI: Multilevel Framework for Shared Authority, Verification, and Skill Preservation
endorsements.quote: At the institutional level, a designated AI governance committee or equivalent multidisciplinary body should approve AI deployment within specific workflows, define local validation requirements, and oversee monitoring and escalation pathways.

evidence.title: Lessons Learned and Iterative Enhancements: A 2-Year Experience with an Established Responsible AI Framework
evidence.effect: Formal evaluation resulted in 50% of tools being approved, 34% conditionally approved, and 13% rejected.
evidence.quote: Across evaluations, 50% were approved, 34% conditionally approved, and 13% rejected.

evidence.title: Factors for Patient Trust and Acceptance of Medical Artificial Intelligence
evidence.effect: Local hospital certification increased preference (AMCE, 0.078 [95% CI, 0.068 to 0.088]) vs uncertified.
evidence.quote: The increase for local hospital certification (AMCE, 0.078 [95% CI, 0.068 to 0.088]) was smaller (difference between local and FDA, 0.033 [95% CI, 0.019 to 0.047]; P < .001; difference between local and Mayo Clinic, 0.034 [95% CI, 0.020 to 0.048]; P < .001).

commentary.bottom_line: Nine frameworks and commentaries endorse formal, risk-tiered approval before deployment, and two studies suggest the process can run in practice and that patients may prefer locally certified tools. No study shows that formal approval reduces patient harm or improves tool performance after deployment, so confidence in the benefit is very low.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice. A pre-post study without a comparator, conducted in a real U.S. deployment, reported that 50% of tools were approved, 34% conditionally approved, and 13% rejected. A vignette survey measured stated patient preference. Neither study measured patient harm or post-deployment performance, so certainty is very low because of study design and indirectness.

Across 64 evaluations, 13% of tools were rejected and 34% received conditions. This suggests the review step may stop or modify some tools before they reach patients. The study did not report whether rejected tools would have caused harm or whether approved tools performed safely afterward.

The review ran in a real deployment, with 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions. This suggests a structured approval process can operate in practice and that some tools may return for repeat review. The study did not report review time, clinician burden, or how consistently risk tiers were applied.

No supplied study reports the cost or staffing required for governance review. The count of 64 evaluations for 55 solutions suggests that repeat review may add work beyond one decision per tool. Leaders may need to plan committee capacity for conditional approvals that require follow-up.

In a vignette survey of 3,000 respondents, local hospital certification increased preference compared with uncertified tools (AMCE 0.078, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.088). A recorded approval may therefore support patient trust. Stated preferences in a simulation may differ from the choices patients make in real care.

Neither study reports whether Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations were represented among patients affected by reviewed tools or among survey respondents. No study tested whether approval criteria examine tool performance in these groups.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or tools with and without formal approval on post-deployment safety incidents, tool performance, or equity gaps. The supplied evidence also does not report the cost, staffing, and time to deployment of a review process, or whether risk-tier thresholds assign review intensity appropriately. Comparative or stepped-wedge designs across several systems could address these questions.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The approval rates come from a U.S. deployment whose setting and patient mix are not described in the supplied data, and the survey sample's composition is also not described. It is therefore unknown whether formal approval works the same way, or builds the same trust, in settings that serve these populations.
